items.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 16, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: the guy I studied with was Eddie Pearson

ctx.x: You’ve been able to take your practical experience as a player and channel it into an educational delivery to the public schools?

For 35 years. I’ve done — or maybe 40 — I’ve done what’s called a lecture- demonstration. I think Billy Taylor started this in the 60s, where we lecture and we demonstrate. And I’ve been doing that constantly, every year, because for me it’s been like a commitment. Naturally education — I’ve done all these Broadway shows and Count Basie and all of that, and I realized that education is the key to it. Because when I first started playing trombone, I think maybe last time I told you when I was 12 years old I played…

items.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I studied with a trombonist named Eddie Pearson.

ctx.x: What attracted you to the music? What drew you into a musical career?

I was born in New Orleans, so that made it easy. Music was everywhere. And New Orleans has been, is and has been a tourist city, so in tourist cities there is much more employment for musicians. So there were a lot of musicians there, and there still are because it still is a place of employment. But music was sort of something you did. Everybody in the block had an instrument. It wasn’t that much — well there were many after school programs. Dance was one, and music certainly was another, and sports. But music…

seemed in my mind that it had taken me 50 years to get from the space back sort of behind stage, to up front. The last time I was there I was in the background playing my little bass drum now here, it’s sort of achieved a little status tonight. It was great for me, you know, everybody wants to look good in their home town. So that happened to me. Actually, to answer your first question, I started playing when I was about eight years old.
